questions.text: Which event in meiosis most directly reduces chromosome number from diploid to haploid?
choices: Separation of sister chromatids in meiosis II
Separation of homologous chromosomes in meiosis I
DNA replication before meiosis
Cytokinesis after fertilization
questions.explain: Meiosis I is the reduction division because homologous chromosomes separate.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. That separates copies but does not first reduce ploidy.
Correct. Homolog separation halves the chromosome number.
Incorrect. Replication duplicates chromosomes without reducing number.
Incorrect. Fertilization restores diploidy rather than reducing it.

mitosis
crossing over

Correct. Crossing over exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes and produces recombinant chromatids.

choices: X-linked recessive
autosomal recessive
mitochondrial
autosomal dominant
questions.explain: The pedigree pattern best fits autosomal dominant inheritance.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. X-linked recessive traits usually affect males more often.
Incorrect. Autosomal recessive traits often skip generations.
Incorrect. Mitochondrial traits follow maternal inheritance patterns.
Correct. Vertical transmission in both sexes is typical of autosomal dominant traits.

questions.text: A karyotype shows three copies of chromosome 21. Which conclusion is correct?
choices: The individual has monosomy 21 because one chromosome is missing
The karyotype proves a point mutation in one gene
The individual has trisomy 21, likely caused by nondisjunction
The extra chromosome resulted from crossing over
questions.explain: Nondisjunction in meiosis can produce gametes with extra chromosomes.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. Three copies indicate trisomy, not monosomy.
Incorrect. Karyotypes show chromosome number and large structure, not single-base changes.
Correct. An extra chromosome 21 is the defining feature of trisomy 21.
Incorrect. Crossing over does not usually change chromosome number.

choices: homozygous recessive × homozygous recessive
heterozygous × homozygous recessive
heterozygous × heterozygous
homozygous dominant × homozygous recessive
questions.explain: A classic 3:1 phenotype pattern points to a heterozygote cross.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. That yields all recessive offspring.
Incorrect. That yields a 1:1 phenotype ratio.

Incorrect. That yields all heterozygous dominant offspring.

questions.text: A chi-square value is very small when observed and expected offspring counts are compared. What conclusion is most supported?
choices: The experiment proves the trait is sex-linked
Independent assortment did not occur because every offspring was identical
The observed data fit the expected ratio reasonably well
The null hypothesis must be rejected immediately
questions.explain: Chi-square helps evaluate whether deviations from expectation are likely due to chance.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. Chi-square alone does not identify sex linkage.
Incorrect. The statistic given does not support that claim.
Correct. A small chi-square means little deviation between observed and expected values.
Incorrect. Large, not tiny, chi-square values are more likely to lead to rejection.

questions.text: Two genes show 12% recombinant offspring. What is the best inference?
choices: The genes are the same gene
Crossing over never occurred
The genes are linked and are about 12 map units apart
The genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently
questions.explain: A recombination frequency well below 50% suggests linkage.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. Recombination frequency does not imply identity.
Incorrect. Recombinants are evidence that crossing over did occur.
Correct. Recombination frequency estimates distance between linked genes.
Incorrect. Independent assortment would give about 50% recombinants.

Height is controlled only by a single dominant allele and never by environment
All plants must have different genotypes because their heights differ
Temperature changes chromosome number in all cells
questions.explain: A norm of reaction describes how one genotype can produce different phenotypes in different environments.

Incorrect. Environmental effects on phenotype do not require chromosome-number changes.

questions.text: A lab tracks chromosome movement and finds daughter cells after meiosis contain one chromosome from each homologous pair. Which conclusion is supported?
choices: Meiosis produces haploid cells
Replication happened after meiosis ended
Mitosis occurred instead of meiosis
Meiosis preserves diploidy in the gametes
questions.explain: Meiosis reduces chromosome number so fertilization can restore diploidy.
choice_explanations: Correct. Homologous chromosomes are separated so gametes carry one member of each pair.
Incorrect. DNA replication occurs before meiosis begins.
Incorrect. The separation of homologs and haploid products indicate meiosis.
Incorrect. Gametes are haploid, not diploid.
questions.image_alt: Diagram of meiosis I and meiosis II showing homologous chromosome separation, sister chromatid separation, and resulting haploid gametes.

questions.text: A cross expected to give a 9:3:3:1 phenotype ratio instead shows many more parental combinations and fewer recombinant combinations. Which explanation is most likely?
choices: The traits are controlled by the same allele

The offspring are all homozygous
questions.explain: Deviation from the independent assortment expectation can reveal linkage.
choice_explanations: Incorrect. Two-trait outcomes indicate distinct loci are being tracked.
Incorrect. Codominance does not specifically produce excess parental classes.
Correct. Linkage causes parental combinations to appear more often than expected under independent assortment.
Incorrect. The pattern described does not imply all offspring are homozygous.

questions.text: An organism with a dominant phenotype is crossed with a homozygous recessive individual and the offspring appear in a 1:1 dominant:recessive ratio. Which genotype did the dominant parent most likely have?
choices: heterozygous

triploid
homozygous recessive
questions.explain: Testcrosses are used to reveal whether a dominant-phenotype individual is heterozygous.
choice_explanations: Correct. A 1:1 phenotype ratio in a testcross indicates the unknown parent was heterozygous.
Incorrect. That would produce all dominant-phenotype offspring.
Incorrect. The ratio described is explained without invoking abnormal ploidy.
Incorrect. The parent had a dominant phenotype, so this is impossible.

Incorrect. Environmental influence does not erase inheritance principles.
Correct. Not every phenotype is determined solely by genotype.
Incorrect. Environmental conditions do not rewrite alleles in this simple way.

questions.text: A dark-fur allele and a light-fur allele are tracked in two habitats, but fur thickness differs mainly with temperature regardless of allele. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Some traits can be strongly influenced by environmental conditions even when genotype is held constant
Temperature changes one allele into another
Genotype never affects phenotype
Mendelian genetics does not apply to any organism in nature
